intro.title: Discover Salinas y Arenales de San Pedro del Pinatar
intro.description: Welcome to the Salinas y Arenales de San Pedro del Pinatar Regional Park, widely recognized as the central Salinas y Arenales de San Pedro del Pinatar. Located in the heart of San Pedro del Pinatar, in the Region of Murcia, Spain, this destination is the natural hub for travelers visiting the area. This unique ecosystem combines salt flats, coastal dunes, and Mediterranean habitats, making it a paradise for nature lovers and birdwatchers.

visitGuide.title: Visit Tips
items: The park is accessible year-round with free admission.
Bring binoculars for excellent birdwatching opportunities.
Wear comfortable shoes for walking on sandy paths.
Visit during sunrise or sunset for the best photography.

alsoKnownAs.title: Highlights
items: Sand dunes of Playa de la Llana

sections.title: Historical Background
sections.content: The salt flats of San Pedro del Pinatar have been in use since ancient times, with evidence of salt production dating back to the Roman era. The park was officially designated as a Regional Park to protect its unique natural and cultural heritage.

sections.title: Ecosystem & Geography
sections.content: The park covers 856 hectares and includes salt flats, coastal lagoons, sand dunes, and pine forests. It serves as a crucial stopover for migratory birds along the Mediterranean flyway.

sections.title: Flora & Fauna
sections.content: The park hosts over 130 species of birds throughout the year, including flamingos, avocets, terns, and gulls. The flora includes salt-tolerant plants, dunes vegetation, and Mediterranean scrubland.

sections.title: Conservation Status
sections.content: The park is protected under multiple international designations: it is a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance, part of the Natura 2000 network as both a Special Protection Area (ZEPA) and a Site of Community Importance (LIC).

sections.title: Visitor Facilities
sections.content: The park features several observation points, walking trails, and an interpretation center. There are information panels along the routes, and guided tours are available upon request.

sections.title: Surroundings & Points of Interest
sections.content: When visiting the Salinas y Arenales de San Pedro del Pinatar Regional Park, visitors can easily explore nearby natural landmarks, including the Mar Menor, the largest coastal lagoon in Europe, and Playa de la Llana, a stretch of protected dunes facing the Mediterranean Sea.

birding.title: Birdwatching Guide: Species & Seasons
birding.subtitle: One of the most important wetland birdwatching sites in the western Mediterranean, with 130+ species recorded yearly
birding.intro: The birds present change noticeably with the seasons. The table below shows the typical seasonal status of common species — 'Common' means easy to see in that season. Bird numbers vary with water levels and from year to year; check on site.
birding.tip: Birdwatching tips: early morning and late afternoon are when birds are most active. Stay quiet, use binoculars or a telephoto lens, never feed or disturb the birds, and keep to the trails and hides.

history.title: History & Legends
history.subtitle: From ancient Roman salt flats to today's internationally protected wetland

eras.title: The Beginnings of Salt Making
eras.content: Salt was one of humanity's earliest trade goods, called 'white gold' by the Romans. Archaeological evidence shows that salt was already being produced from the coastal pans here in Roman times. Roman roads linked the interior to this coast, and salt was shipped across the Empire from these flats.

eras.title: The Golden Age of Salt-Pan Technology
eras.content: During Al-Andalus, Moorish engineers brought advanced water-management and evaporation techniques, turning the old coastal pans into a systematic network of evaporation ponds. The very name 'Salinas' (salt pans) grew out of this long and inseparable local tradition of salt making.

eras.title: The Crown's 'Salt Tax'
eras.content: In the late Middle Ages and early modern period, salt was a royal monopoly in the Kingdom of Castile. The salt flats of San Pedro del Pinatar operated as a royal saltern, becoming a significant source of Crown revenue. The transport and sale of salt were tightly controlled, and smuggling it was a serious crime.

eras.title: Modern Salt Industry and the Seaside Town
eras.content: From the 19th century onward, salt production became industrialized and output grew sharply. Around the salt flats and fishing, San Pedro del Pinatar gradually grew from a fishing hamlet into a coastal town. Salineros (salt workers), fishermen, and sailors form the earliest social memory of the area.

eras.title: Birth of the Regional Park
eras.content: To protect this unique mosaic of salt pans, dunes, and wetlands, the Regional Government of Murcia designated the area a 'Regional Park' (Parque Regional) in 1985 — among the first protected areas in Spain centred on salt-marsh wetlands.

eras.title: International Wetland Protection
eras.content: In 1994 the park was listed under the Ramsar Convention as a Wetland of International Importance, and it is also part of the EU Natura 2000 network (a Special Protection Area, ZEPA, and a Site of Community Importance, LIC). Today it is one of the most important flamingo and migratory-bird habitats on the western Mediterranean coast.

legend.title: Place Names & Local Legends
legend.nameOrigin: 'Saint Peter' and the 'Pine Grove' in the Town's Name
legend.nameOriginContent: 'San Pedro' (Saint Peter) refers to the patron saint of fishermen in Catholic tradition — locally, fishermen traditionally prayed for his protection before setting out to sea, and the Fiestas de San Pedro in late June are still the town's liveliest festival. 'Pinatar' comes from the Latin 'pinus' (pine), referring to the coastal pine groves and dunes. Together, 'Saint Peter's Pine Grove' captures both the fishing and the natural heritage of this coast.
legend.saltLegend: The 'White Gold' Legend of the Salt Pans
legend.saltLegendContent: An old saying has been passed down among salineros (salt workers) for generations: 'Salt is the sweat left behind by the sun.' Legend has it that at the height of summer the sun pours its warmth into the pans, letting salt crystals grow on the bed like snow — and the family that harvests its pans before autumn gains salt that is especially white and commands the highest price. Romantic as it is, the tale reflects how deeply this community valued its salt, the lifeblood of this coast for centuries.
legend.note: Note: These legends are local folklore passed down by word of mouth, shared here for cultural reference only.

saltMaking.title: How Salt Is Made: How the Salt Pans Work
saltMaking.subtitle: Turning seawater into sea salt with the sun, the wind, and an age-old 'concentration line'
saltMaking.intro: The salt pans of this park still use the traditional solar-evaporation method: seawater flows through a series of shallow ponds, evaporates and concentrates, and finally crystallizes into salt — almost entirely powered by natural energy.

steps.title: Drawing in the seawater
steps.content: Using tides or the traditional windmills, seawater is taken from the Mar Menor or the Mediterranean into the first storage ponds, where it settles and clarifies.

steps.title: Concentration by evaporation
steps.content: The water moves through successive shallow ponds. With large surfaces and a thin water layer, sun and wind speed up evaporation, raising salinity from about 3.5% in the sea to near saturation.

steps.title: Crystallization
steps.content: When the brine is nearly saturated it is fed into the shallowest crystallization ponds. As the water keeps evaporating, sodium chloride crystallizes first, forming snow-white salt on the bottom.

steps.title: Harvesting and stacking
steps.content: Salt workers gather the crystals with wooden rakes and pile them at the edge to drain and dry before bagging. Harvesting usually takes place from summer to early autumn.

steps.title: A shared ecosystem
steps.content: The ponds are also wetland habitat: the varying salinities support salt-tolerant algae, brine shrimp, and halophytes — which give some ponds their pink colour and attract flamingos to feed.

saltMaking.note: Note: The exact workings of the saltern and the areas open to visitors may change — check on site or with official sources.

transport.title: How to Get Here
transport.fromCenterDesc: Approximately 45km from Murcia city center. Take the A-7 motorway towards Cartagena, then exit towards San Pedro del Pinatar.
transport.fromStationDesc: About 20km from Cartagena. Accessible by bus or car via the RM-3 and AP-7.
transport.fromAirportDesc: Murcia International Airport (RMU) is approximately 15km away. Alicante Airport (ALC) is about 75km north.
transport.publicTransportDesc: Interurban buses connect San Pedro del Pinatar with Murcia and Cartagena. Local buses serve the town.
transport.walkingDesc: The park is accessible on foot from San Pedro del Pinatar town center (approximately 2km to the main entrance).
transport.drivingDesc: Accessible by car via the AP-7 or RM-3. Follow signs to 'Salinas' or 'Parque Regional'.

route.title: Recommended Route
route.overview: A scenic walk through the salt flats and coastal dunes.
steps: Start at the main parking area near the interpretation center
Walk along the southern observation trail for birdwatching
Visit the salt flats and observe traditional salt harvesting
Continue to the dunes of Playa de la Llana
End at the northern lookout point for sunset views

trails.title: Trails at a Glance & Difficulty
trails.subtitle: Choose a route that fits your time and fitness
trails.intro: The park is mostly flat salt pans and dunes, so most paths are easy. Below are the common route types — lengths and times are approximate; always follow the signs on site.

trails.name: Salt Pan Loop (Ruta Salinera)
trails.desc: Start near the interpretation center and circle the ponds to watch traditional salt making, passing several bird hides. The most popular introductory route.

trails.name: Llana Coastal Trail (Camino de la Llana)
trails.desc: Runs along the coastal dunes to Playa de la Llana facing the Mediterranean. Walking on sand takes a bit more effort, but the views and sunsets are superb.

trails.name: Cabezo de la Fuente Lookout
trails.desc: Climb the park's small hill for panoramic views over the salt pans, lagoons, and the Mar Menor. Some elevation gain; great for those who like heights.

trails.name: Windmill & Seafront Loop (Molino de Quintín)
trails.desc: Links the traditional salt windmill, bird hides, and the Mar Menor seafront, with plenty of info panels — great for families on foot or by bike.

trails.note: Tip: in summer start early to avoid the heat; sandy paths can be slippery after rain — wear grippy shoes and carry water.

spots.title: Salt Flats Lookout
spots.description: The view of the salt flats with pink waters during evaporation season creates stunning reflections, especially at sunrise.

spots.title: Bird Hide (Observatorio)
spots.description: One of several birdwatching hides around the lagoons. Perfect for capturing flamingos and other wading birds.

spots.title: Playa de la Llana Dunes
spots.description: The sand dunes offer beautiful textures and coastal views, ideal for landscape and nature photography.

spots.title: Sunset Viewpoint
spots.description: The northern part of the park offers panoramic sunset views over the salt flats and the Mar Menor.

facilities.title: Visitor Facilities & Services
facilities.subtitle: Neutral, objective facility types — no specific businesses are recommended
facilities.intro: Below are the common types of services available in and around the park. Availability may vary; always check on site or with official sources.

items.title: Public Restrooms (WC)
items.desc: Public restrooms are available near the main entrances, the interpretation center, and some birdwatching points. During peak summer hours they can get busy.
items.tip: Tip: Some remote trail sections have no restrooms — plan ahead.

items.title: Parking
items.desc: The park has several free parking areas, including a main lot near the interpretation center. Spaces fill quickly on weekends and in summer, so arrive early.
items.tip: Tip: Never park on sand or outside designated areas — you may get stuck or damage the dunes.

items.title: Dining
items.desc: There are no restaurants inside the park. The town of San Pedro del Pinatar and the seafront boulevard offer a wide choice of Mediterranean restaurants, cafés, snack bars, and ice-cream shops.
items.tip: Tip: Open fires and large picnics are not allowed in most of the park — take your rubbish with you.

items.title: Accommodation
items.desc: San Pedro del Pinatar and the Lo Pagán seaside district offer several types of accommodation, from hotels and aparthotels to holiday apartments and guesthouses, across all budgets.
items.tip: Tip: Summer is high season — booking in advance is strongly recommended.

items.title: Supermarkets & Everyday Services
items.desc: The town center has supermarkets, bakeries, butcher shops, pharmacies, and convenience stores where visitors can stock up on water, food, and sun protection.
items.tip: Tip: Pharmacies (Farmacia) are good places for sunscreen and insect repellent.

items.title: Fuel & EV Charging
items.desc: Petrol stations are available in town and along the AP-7 / RM-3 roads, several with convenience stores. EV drivers can find public charging points in town and in nearby urban areas.
items.tip: Tip: Fill up before entering the park — fuel points are scarce on rural roads.

myths.title: Common Myths & Facts
myths.subtitle: About the salt pans and the park — are these claims actually true?

items.myth: "The water in the salt pans is pink because colour has been added."
items.fact: No. The pink comes from salt-tolerant algae (Dunaliella salina) and halophilic microbes in the highly saline water; their natural pigments tint the ponds, and the colour deepens with salinity.

items.myth: "If I go, I'm guaranteed to see the pink lagoon."
items.fact: Not always. The pink is mainly visible during the evaporation/concentration phase (usually summer to early autumn) and depends on water levels and temperature. The pans have plenty to see all year — the pink is just one highlight.
No. The park is free and open to everyone all year round; some guided activities run by the authorities are separate from any entrance fee.

items.myth: "You can freely walk into the dunes and the ponds."
items.fact: No. The ponds are working and ecological areas, mostly closed to the public, and dune vegetation is fragile. Stay on trails and viewing platforms to help protect bird habitat.
Flamingos are mainly migratory and wintering birds, most numerous in autumn and winter, with fewer in spring and summer. For large flocks, visit in winter or during the spring/autumn migrations.

items.myth: "You can swim directly in the salt ponds."
items.fact: No. The ponds are production facilities and swimming is not allowed. Swim at proper beaches such as Playa de la Llana or the Mar Menor shore.

items.q: Where is the Salinas y Arenales de San Pedro del Pinatar Regional Park located?
items.a: It is located in San Pedro del Pinatar, Region of Murcia, Spain (postal code 30740), between the Mar Menor lagoon and the Mediterranean Sea.

items.q: Is Salinas y Arenales de San Pedro del Pinatar free to visit?
items.a: Yes, the park is a public space and is free to visit year-round, open 24 hours a day.

items.q: What birds can you see at the park?
items.a: More than 130 species of birds can be observed throughout the year, including flamingos, avocets, terns, and gulls, especially during spring and autumn migration.

items.q: Are there restrooms and dining facilities inside the park?
items.a: Public restrooms are available near the main entrances and the interpretation center, but there are no restaurants inside the park. Dining, accommodation, supermarkets, and other daily services are concentrated in the town of San Pedro del Pinatar and the seafront area, with a wide range of options.

items.q: Besides flamingos, what else can you see at the park?
items.a: More than 130 bird species are recorded in the park each year. Besides flamingos, look out for avocets, black-winged stilts, terns, egrets, and several gulls, plus reptiles and amphibians around the dunes, and extensive salt-tolerant plants and Mediterranean scrub.

items.q: Is the park suitable for families with children or visitors with reduced mobility?
items.a: Yes. The park has several flat, easy trails, and the main parking area gives straightforward access to the interpretation center and bird hides. Sandy paths can be more tiring, so it is best to ask the interpretation center or check official trail information to choose a route that suits your group.

officialManagement.title: About Salinas y Arenales
officialManagement.text: The Salinas y Arenales de San Pedro del Pinatar Regional Park is a protected natural area in the Region of Murcia, Spain. The park is managed by the Regional Government of Murcia in collaboration with the San Pedro del Pinatar Town Council for conservation and public use.
